# Readers, writers and texts
## The area of exploration
Readers, writers and texts asks how meaning is made between a writer, a text and a reader. It focuses on the choices writers make and the way readers respond. Guiding questions include: why and how do we study literature, and how are we affected by literary texts?

## Key ideas
Authorial choices are the decisions a writer makes about form, structure and language. Reader response is the idea that readers create meaning based on their own experiences. Close reading is the careful analysis of a short passage. Literary features include imagery, diction, tone, symbolism, narrative voice and structure. Always link a feature to its effect on the reader.

## Non-literary texts
In Language and Literature you study non-literary bodies of work as well as literary works. A non-literary text is a text such as an advertisement, speech, article, infographic or website. A body of work is a collection of non-literary texts by one creator or on one topic. Analyse how its purpose, audience and context shape its stylistic features.

## Key terms
Authorial choice: a decision a writer makes about form, structure or language
Reader response: the idea that readers help create meaning
Close reading: careful analysis of a short passage
Diction: the writer’s choice of words
Tone: the writer’s attitude conveyed through language
Imagery: language that appeals to the senses
Non-literary text: a text such as an advert, speech or article
Body of work: a collection of non-literary texts by one creator or on one topic

# Time and space
## The area of exploration
Time and space asks how texts are shaped by and shape their contexts. It considers the historical, cultural and social settings in which texts are written and read. Guiding questions include: how important is cultural or historical context to the production and reception of a text?

## Key ideas
Context of production is the time, place and culture in which a text was written. Context of reception is the situation in which a reader reads it. Texts can reflect, challenge or reshape the values of their time. Works in translation help you explore how culture shapes literature. A perspective is a particular way of seeing an issue, shaped by context.

## Non-literary texts
In Language and Literature you study non-literary bodies of work as well as literary works. A non-literary text is a text such as an advertisement, speech, article, infographic or website. A body of work is a collection of non-literary texts by one creator or on one topic. Analyse how its purpose, audience and context shape its stylistic features.

## Key terms
Context of production: the time and culture in which a text was written
Context of reception: the situation in which a text is read
Perspective: a particular way of seeing, shaped by context
Work in translation: a literary work originally written in another language
Non-literary text: a text such as an advert, speech or article
Body of work: a collection of non-literary texts by one creator or on one topic
Intertextuality: connecting texts:
# Intertextuality: connecting texts
## The area of exploration
Intertextuality asks how texts relate to each other. It explores shared conventions, themes and techniques across works. Guiding questions include: how do texts adhere to and deviate from conventions, and how do comparisons offer new insight?

## Key ideas
Intertextuality is the relationship between texts, through allusion, adaptation, parody or shared themes. An allusion is a brief reference to another text, person or event. Genre conventions are the typical features of a type of text, such as the sonnet or the tragedy. A global issue is a significant, transnational issue that appears in many texts and connects them, such as identity, power or conflict.

## Non-literary texts
In Language and Literature you study non-literary bodies of work as well as literary works. A non-literary text is a text such as an advertisement, speech, article, infographic or website. A body of work is a collection of non-literary texts by one creator or on one topic. Analyse how its purpose, audience and context shape its stylistic features.

## Key terms
Intertextuality: the relationship between texts
Allusion: a brief reference to another text, person or event
Genre: a category of text with shared conventions
Convention: a typical feature of a genre
Parody: an imitation of a text for comic or critical effect
Global issue: a significant transnational issue explored across texts
Non-literary text: a text such as an advert, speech or article
Body of work: a collection of non-literary texts by one creator or on one topic

# Paper 1: guided textual analysis (non-literary)
## The paper
Paper 1 gives you unseen non-literary texts, each with a guiding question. At SL you analyse one text in 1 hour 15 minutes; at HL you analyse two in 2 hours 15 minutes. Text types include advertisements, opinion columns, speeches, infographics, cartoons, blogs and photographs with captions.

## How to answer
Identify the text type, purpose, audience and context. Build a thesis that answers the guiding question. Analyse how stylistic and structural features — such as layout, images, typography, rhetorical devices and tone — create meaning and effect. Rhetorical devices include ethos, pathos and logos, rhetorical questions and repetition. Embed short quotations and refer to visual features precisely.

## Key terms
Text type: the kind of text, such as an advert or speech
Purpose: what a text aims to do, such as persuade or inform
Audience: the people a text is aimed at
Ethos: persuasion through credibility
Pathos: persuasion through emotion
Logos: persuasion through logic and evidence
Paper 2: comparative essay:
# Paper 2: comparative essay
## The paper
Paper 2 is a comparative essay on two works you have studied, answering one of four general questions, in 1 hour 45 minutes. You cannot use works from your individual oral or HL essay.

## How to answer
Choose the question that best fits your two works. Plan a comparative thesis. Integrate comparison throughout using connectives such as similarly, whereas and in contrast, rather than writing about each work separately. Use remembered quotations and specific references to plot, characters and techniques. Show how each writer's choices create meaning.

## Key terms
Comparative essay: an essay that analyses two works together
Comparative thesis: an argument that relates both works to the question
Integrated comparison: comparing works within each paragraph
Whereas: a connective showing contrast

# Individual oral
## The assessment
The individual oral is the internal assessment. You speak for 10 minutes, followed by 5 minutes of teacher questions, about how a global issue is presented in an extract from a literary work and an extract from a non-literary body of work.

## How to prepare
Choose a specific global issue present in both texts. Select extracts of up to 40 lines each, or a single non-literary text. Prepare an outline of up to 10 bullet points. Explain how each creator presents the issue through stylistic choices, and connect each extract to the whole work or body of work.

## Key terms
Global issue: a significant, transnational issue present in both texts
Extract: a short passage of up to 40 lines
Outline: up to 10 bullet points used during the oral
Stylistic choice: a decision about language, structure or visuals
HL essay:
# HL essay
## The essay
The HL essay is a formal essay of 1200–1500 words on one literary work or non-literary body of work studied in the course. It develops a line of inquiry and is externally assessed.

## How to do well
Choose a narrow, arguable line of inquiry. Build a clear thesis and support it with close analysis of language, structure and, for non-literary texts, visual features. Use secondary sources only to support your own argument and cite them properly. Organize the essay with topic sentences and a conclusion that answers the line of inquiry.

## Key terms
Line of inquiry: the focused question your essay investigates
Formal essay: an academic essay with a clear argument
Secondary source: criticism or research about the text
Topic sentence: the first sentence of a paragraph stating its point
